title: the mudras
hook: a raised open palm on a temple image, and a lowered one beneath it: two hands that speak first
carry: the raised palm that says do not fear

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breathing hand: two fingers folded, the thumb and ring finger steering the breath, one nostril, then the other. Today the hands turn around and face you.

A crossing guard steps into the road and lifts one hand, palm out, fingers up. The cars stop. Nobody says a word. Now stand before an image of Shiva as the dancer, ringed in flame. Among his hands, one is raised, open, palm toward you, fingers up. Almost the crossing guard's hand. But it isn't saying stop. It's saying something gentler. So far the mudras have been things a practitioner does. Today, two you don't make. You receive them.
screen: `ONE RAISED PALM STOPS THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE SAME PALM ON SHIVA.` → `A MUDRA YOU RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: That raised, open palm is abhaya mudra. Abhaya means fearlessness, the absence of fear. The gesture says: do not be afraid. On some images, look for a second hand, lowered, palm open toward you, fingers pointing down, as if letting something fall into your hands. That's varada mudra, the gesture of giving, of granting what is asked. In some paintings of Lakshmi, coins pour from that lowered palm. One hand lifts the fear. The other gives. Now open the Bhagavad Gita to its sixteenth chapter. Krishna lists the qualities of a person whose nature leans toward the divine, and the list begins with one word: abhayam, fearlessness. Then purity of heart, steadiness in knowledge, giving, self-control. So when a devotee stands before that raised hand, the very quality the Gita names first is being held out to them. People read the gesture in more than one way. Some hear a promise: the god protects, there's nothing to fear here. Some hear an invitation: this is a quality meant to grow in the one who looks. The palm holds both. One more detail: the same raised palm and lowered, giving hand also appear on Buddhist and Jain images, each tradition reading them in its own way. A shared language of hands. And it turns the mudras around. They aren't only something you form in a quiet room. You stand in front of a hand, and it speaks first.
screen: `ABHAYA: THE PALM THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.` · `VARADA: THE LOWERED PALM THAT GIVES.` · `GITA 16: THE LIST OPENS WITH FEARLESSNESS.` · `A PROMISE, OR AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `THE HAND SPEAKS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let the left hand rest beside the left knee, palm open and turned forward, fingers down: the giving hand. Raise the right hand to shoulder height, palm forward, fingers up and relaxed: the hand that says do not fear. Breathe slowly, and if a worry comes, let it meet the raised palm without arguing; if you pray, you can face a home shrine, and if not, just let the hands rest in their shapes.
The mudras. Today, two you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the lowered palm that gives.
Your line: the raised palm that says do not fear. Tomorrow, the hands go on stage. Day one thousand thirty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Devotees meet abhaya and varada mudras on the images of deities in temples and home shrines; the raised open palm is read as "do not fear" and the lowered open palm as the giving of blessings.
